newsitem.title: FINLAND: Finnish rating upgrade would be justified-Niinisto.
newsitem.headline: Finnish rating upgrade would be justified-Niinisto.

text.p: Finance Minister Sauli Niinisto was quoted on Wednesday by Finnish radio as saying an upgrade of Finland's credit rating would be justified.
Finance Ministry officials have said that rating institute Standard and Poor's visited Finland last week, and Moody's was due to visit this week.
The radio news said both S&P and Moody's would release new reports on Finland before Christmas.
"According to Finance Minister Sauli Niinisto, a rise in Finland's credit rating would be justified," the radio news said, referring to an interview with him.
Niinisto told the radio an upgrade could reduce Finnish state debt servicing expenditure by "billions of markka".

At end-October, Finnish state debt was 397.71 billion markka. The foreign currency debt -- the primary focus of interest for international credit rating agencies -- was 173.04 billion markka, according to State Treasury Office data.
In 1997, state debt servicing spending will rise to about 31 billion markka, or some 15.5 percent of total state budget expenditure, from 29 billion in 1996.

S&P's current foreign currency loan rating for Finland is AA minus and its outlook was changed to positive from stable in August last year. Moody's Aa2 rating has been unchanged since January 1992. Rating institute IBCA in March this year gave Finland an AA rating and said the outlook was positive.
Senior Finnish finance ministry officials started voicing hopes of a credit upgrade in autumn 1994, but added that it might take time for this to materialise.

Since then, Finland has joined the European Union, reduced inflation to below one percent, linked the earlier floating markka to the ERM, severely cut budget spending and reduced the budget deficit towards the three percent deficit to GDP ratio required by the Maastricht Treaty for membership of Economic and Monetary Union.
Finland is set to fulfil in 1997 all criteria for membership of the third phase of EMU, except gross public debt to GDP, which is projected to be slightly above the 60 percent limit.
The government's stated objective is that Finland should join the single currency from the scheduled January 1999 start.
